title: What Is H2F?
text: Perfect. Thank you, Kathy-Lynn. Um, hi everybody. Like Kathy-Lynn mentioned, my name is Dr. Rosie Catinoso, and I serve as the director of human performance operations. Uh, I'm also a physical therapist, and I've had the privilege of working on the H2F program at Fort Bragg. Uh, so I'm really excited to be here and get the opportunity to share all of the great things that H2F has to offer, as well as give a deep dive into what the athletic training position entails. So, first thing we'll talk about is what is the actual concept of H2F. So, H2F really stems from the Army's intent to shift the military health care model from one that was traditionally reactive, where we would really just wait around for soldiers to get hurt before we would intervene in any way, to a much more proactive approach. The mindset stems from professional sports. You know, we surround athletes with teams of health care providers and human performance experts so that they can be the best in the soccer arena or on the football field. Why not take that same concept and apply it to our soldiers so that they can be the best in the tactical space. The program started back in 2018 as a pilot where they had a few select units that were provided H2F resources to see if this program had any legs, if it, you know, was going to be successful. So, not only did providing H2F resources to those units decrease injury rates, but it also increased fitness scores and increased overall unit readiness and deployability. So, the Army saw the H2F concept as a win and decided to green light it in its full capacity, which is where we are today. So, next I'll talk about what actually makes up the H2F team and the different domains that it consists of.

title: The Five Domains of Soldier Readiness
text: So, the idea behind H2F is that there are five domains in a soldier's life and if a soldier addresses each one of those equally, that's what will promote optimal health and wellness. First domain we're going to talk about is the physical readiness domain. And this is where athletic trainers will fall. Physical readiness can really be looked at in two different categories. So, on one hand, it's going to be the physical training of our soldiers. So, that's how they exercise and stay active. That is the primary responsibility of the strength and conditioning coaches, and it's their job to develop and implement periodized workout programs so that our soldiers are training effectively and training efficiently. The other side of physical readiness is the injury prevention and injury response team, and that's where our athletic trainers, our physical therapists, and our physical therapy specialists are focused. Their primary role is to respond to musculoskeletal injuries as soon as they happen so that we can initiate the recovery process day one rather than having to wait 3 to 4 weeks for that individual to get into the traditional clinics on post. Uh they're also responsible for injury prevention initiatives. So, the goal of H2F really is to be proactive and get on the front side of our soldiers' injuries. So, with that, the ATs, the PTs, and the physical therapy specialists will create a variety of different educational opportunities so that our soldiers have a better understanding of how to care for themselves, which should help decrease injuries in the long run. Next, we'll talk about the mental readiness and the sleep readiness domain. Uh so, mental readiness is all about training our brains in the same way we train our bodies. Uh so, we work out to be physically fit. Let's train our brains to be mentally fit. Mental readiness includes things like mental toughness. So, how do we build up our soldiers' abilities to push through and do hard things? Um we want them to obviously be able to physically conquer a task, um but we need them to be able to mentally do that, too. It also includes things like mental resiliency. So, how do we make sure our soldiers are prepared to get back on the horse uh if and when they say uh face a setback. Uh and then it also covers things like stress management techniques, uh instilling healthy coping mechanisms in our soldiers so that they're able to handle um all of the ins and outs that that come with being a soldier. Uh going hand-in-hand with mental readiness, we also have the sleep readiness domain. And sleep readiness is all about making sure our soldiers get enough sleep and they get quality sleep. Uh the big emphasis with sleep readiness is to educate leadership on the importance of sleep, uh that it is something that we all need in order to perform at our best, and it's something that we should be prioritizing in our training programs. Sleep readiness will also work with the soldiers one-on-one or in group formats to educate them on different ways they can optimize the quality and quantity of their sleep. Mental readiness and sleep readiness will be covered by occupational therapists, occupational therapy specialists, and cognitive performance specialists. Next up, we have nutritional readiness, and the saying I like to use for nutritional readiness is, if you give a man a fish, you feed him for a day, but if you teach a man to fish, you feed him for life. So, the goal of nutritional readiness is to educate and empower our soldiers to make smart choices about how they fuel their bodies. It's to give them the tools that they need, so when they're in the dining facility, they can make a well-balanced meal that's going to fuel them for all of their activities that they'll be doing throughout that work day. Nutritional readiness has the opportunity to work on three different levels. So, the dieticians can work one-on-one with soldiers to help them meet whatever their nutritional goals might be. They can do body composition assessments. They can order labs to determine if there's any nutritional deficiencies. They can develop meal plans, and really tailor their services to the specifics of that patient. Second, they'll work at the unit level, and this is where they do a lot of the education, you know, presenting to groups so that they're providing that evidence-based information, and our soldiers are getting good quality info on, you know, what they should be focusing on from a nutrition standpoint. And then third, they'll also work at the installation level to increase access to healthy foods. So, that might be working with the dining facilities to make sure that healthy food foods are available at each meal time, that foods are labeled appropriately. We've even had some teams that have worked with vending machine companies on post to make sure that healthy options are available wherever the soldiers might be, so it shouldn't be a hard choice for them to make. And then last but not least, we have the spiritual readiness domain. And spiritual readiness develops the connection that gives meaning and purpose to one's life. It's to help soldiers build out core values, beliefs, and identities that are unique to the soldiers but common to all. It really provides resiliency in times of stress, hardship, and tragedy. [clears throat Spiritual readiness will be primarily spearheaded by the chaplains which are military religious figures. So, all of the providers that you see listed here make up the H2F team and those are individuals that you would be working alongside of if you were to come on board as part of the H2F program. Now,

title: What Athletic Trainers Do in H2F
text: one of the questions we always get is, you know, what does an athletic trainer do within the H2F program? So, there are three primary roles that are ATs really focus on within their respective H2F team. First is the athletic trainers will provide athletic training coverage to army training events. So, this is going to be more of that traditional AT experience that you would see on the sidelines of practices or games. The only difference is that our ATs are on the sidelines of different army events. So, that could be anything from a physical fitness test, a run, an obstacle course, to even you know, a flag football game that they might be doing for the holidays as a a team building activity. ATs are on the sidelines and able to respond to injuries if and when they happen as well as support other medical personnel who may be at those events as well. This first picture that you see here on the left, this is actually Megan. She had the opportunity to observe a field training exercise and ride in a Humvee. So, really cool unique opportunities to witness you know, different army trainings as part of the athletic training role. Second primary responsibility is to evaluate and treat a variety of musculoskeletal injuries. So, our athletic trainers are typically the first person that a soldier is seeing for their musculoskeletal complaint. They're performing initial evaluation, determining diagnosis, developing a plan of care, and then taking that soldier through the course of their recovery. So, it is a direct access environment, and our ATs do have a lot of clinical autonomy to evaluate and treat patients as they see fit. Now, they're not alone on an island. They do have support from other medical providers. They'll work closely with their physical therapists, with their unit primary care providers, but they're going to be the the main person that is addressing acute musculoskeletal injuries within the unit. And then third, our athletic trainers provide injury prevention education, classes, screenings. Again, trying to shift that proactive approach to health care. Our ATs work with their soldiers to identify anybody who might be at an increased risk of injury and work with them before the injuries happen, as well as share knowledge on how to better care for yourselves. The second picture that you see here, this is from Cass. She was out there leading a morning mobility PT session. So, making sure that our soldiers have a good understanding of appropriate warm-up, cool-down, and mobility techniques so they can train appropriately. Overall, the athletic trainers are focused on optimizing soldier performance within their army unit. Each army unit might do that a little bit differently, but overall, that's going to be the primary focus and goal of our athletic trainers working within H2F. Now, I'm going to hand it over to Cass, and she's going to walk you through what
